title: Improvement of anti-swelling property and anticorrosion performance of epoxy coatings by the introduction of nanocrystalline cellulose composite.

sections.heading: Materials and methods
sections.text: Materials and methods Materials Sodium chloride, DMF, ethyl acetate, anhydrous ethanol, 3-aminopropyltrimethoxysilane (APTMS), hexadecyltrimethoxysilane (HDTMS), aqueous ammonia (28%), epoxy resin (E-44) and curing agent were purchased from Aladdin. Q235 carbon steel was purchased from Xincheng Senke Specimen Processing Center. NCC was purchased from Northern Century (Jiangsu) Cellulose Material Co., Ltd. Preparation of M-NCC epoxy solution 1.25 g, 2.5 g, 7.5 g and 12.5 g of NCC solution (with a 2% NCC content) were separately weighed, corresponding to absolute dry masses of NCC at 0.025 g, 0.05 g, 0.15 g and 0.25 g, respectively. These were then dispersed in anhydrous ethanol. The NCC-ethanol solutions with varying contents were centrifuged at 9000 rpm for 15 min. The resulting precipitates were collected and transferred to 30 mL of anhydrous ethanol, and 0.1 g of HDTMS, 0.05 g of 3 APTMS and 1 mL of ammonia water were added. The NCC was modified under magnetic stirring for 1 h. Subsequently, 5 g of epoxy resin E-44 was added and stirred for 15 min to yield NCC epoxy solutions with mass fractions of 0.5%, 1%, 3% and 5%, respectively (where 0.5%, 1%, 3% and 5% represent the mass ratios of the absolute dry NCC to the epoxy resin). Preparation of M-NCC epoxy coating The epoxy resin with a mass ratio of epoxy resin E-44 to curing agent of 4 :1 was prepared, and 30 mL ethyl acetate was added and stirred evenly. Ethyl acetate was used as a solvent. The epoxy coating primer was prepared on pre-polished Q235 carbon steel by the dip-coating method. The thickness of the epoxy coating was 10 ± 2 μm. Different content of M-NCC epoxy solution was added to the air compressor sprayer and sprayed on Q235 carbon steel with epoxy coating primer, and cured at 90 °C for 6 h in an oven to prepare epoxy composite coatings doped with 0.5%, 1%, 3%, and 5% alkoxysilane coupling agent M-NCC, namely M-0.5% NCC/EP, M-1% NCC/EP, M-3% NCC/EP, and M-5% NCC/EP coatings. The coating thickness was 75 ± 5 μm. Preparation of pure epoxy coating An epoxy-ethyl acetate solution consisting of 5 g epoxy resin E-44 and 30 mL ethyl acetate was sprayed on Q235 carbon steel with a 10 ± 2 μm epoxy coating and cured at 90 °C for 6 h in an oven to prepare a pure epoxy coating with a coating thickness of 75 ± 5 μm. Electrochemical measurements A three-electrode system was employed, including a saturated calomel electrode as the reference electrode, a platinum black electrode as the counter electrode, and a Q235 carbon steel electrode with a coating as the working electrode. EIS measurements were conducted using a Princeton VersaSTAT 3 F electrochemical workstation with an applied amplitude of 20 mV, a frequency range of 10 4  ~10 − 2 , and 10 points per frequency doubling. The corrosion process was analyzed by establishing an equivalent circuit diagram and fitting the data using the ZView software. Characterizations The differences in chemical bonds of the samples were characterized using Fourier Transform Infrared Reflection (FTIR, IRPrestige-21) spectroscopy. The TGA and DTG measurements were obtained using a thermogravimetric analyzer (TGA8000) at a heating rate of 10 °C min-1 under a nitrogen atmosphere (50 mL/min). FESEM (Quanta FEG 250, FEI, USA) was employed to characterize the sample morphology, element content and distribution analysis (EDS and element mapping). X-ray photoelectron spectra (XPS) were acquired using an X-ray photoelectron spectrometer (AXIS Ultra DLD, Kratos Co., England), employing monochromatic Al Kα radiation (1486.6 eV) as the excitation source. The binding energy was calibrated to 284.6 eV for the C 1s peak. The water contact angle (WCA) was measured and calculated on a contact angle measuring instrument (ZJ-7000, Zhijia Instruments, China) using the dynamic mode, where a drop of 5 µL water was dispensed onto the thin film surface by an automatic piston syringe and immediately photographed. The 3D optical topography of the samples was measured using a 3D optical profiler (Up S-Dual, RTEC, USA) and visualized using Gwyddion software (version 2.44). The optical images of the samples were captured using an optical electronic microscope ( AO-HD208C, AOSVI, China).

Introduction Metal corrosion has long been a stubborn and widespread problem in the industrial domain. Particularly in extreme conditions marked by high temperatures, high humidity, and high salinity, the corrosion rate of metal materials escalates significantly, posing substantial threats to the safe operation of equipment and structures 1 , 2 . E Epoxy resin coatings, commonly employed as a protective material for metals, offer superior adhesion and electrical insulation properties. However, their protective efficacy is often undermined in extremely corrosive environments 3 , especially for metal hot-end components like those in marine engines (Liu et al. 4 . These components are exposed to alternating high and low temperatures in a marine salt spray environment over prolonged periods 5 , causing the coatings to age and crack, which subsequently leads to the corrosion of the metal substrate 6 . Thus, enhancing the anti-corrosion performance of epoxy resin coatings under extreme conditions is crucial for prolonging the service life of metal materials. In extreme corrosive settings, the performance of epoxy resin coatings deteriorates markedly due to the combined influence of multiple factors 7 – 10 . These include lapses in the construction process, drastic temperature fluctuations in the environment, frequent humidity alterations, intense chemical corrosion, inevitable physical shock damage, and the aging of the material itself. These factors collectively act on the coating, resulting in structural flaws such as micropores and cracks within it. These defects not only compromise the coating’s integrity but also provide a penetration route for the corrosive medium, intensifying the accumulation of interfacial stress between the coating and the metal substrate. As these defects and stresses persist and worsen, the protective performance of the coating is severely weakened, eventually leading to coating failure and accelerating the corrosion of the metal substrate. Nanofillers have demonstrated a considerable impact on enhancing coating performance due to their distinctive size and surface effects. The introduction of nanofillers can effectively fill the micropores and cracks within the coating, significantly reduce the permeability of the corrosive medium, and notably enhance the interfacial bonding between the coating and the metal substrate, thereby minimizing the generation of interfacial stress. Specifically, carbon-based nanofillers like graphene and carbon nanotubes can effectively improve the wear resistance and corrosion resistance of coatings thanks to their excellent conductivity and mechanical strength, enabling them to have a longer service life in extreme conditions 11 , 12 . Metal-based nanofillers, particularly silver nanoparticles, exhibit excellent performance in preventing microbial-induced corrosion due to their outstanding antibacterial properties 13 , 12 . Polymer-based nanofillers, such as polytetrafluoroethylene nanoparticles, can significantly enhance the hydrophobicity and chemical corrosion resistance of coatings, ensuring their stability in diverse chemical environments 14 , 15 . Despite the numerous benefits brought by nanofiller grafting to coating performance, we must also confront the challenges it poses in practical applications. Issues such as the dispersibility and stability of nanofillers, along with their compatibility with the epoxy resin matrix, frequently restrict their performance in coatings 16 – 18 . Therefore, one of the current research focuses is to identify more suitable nanofillers, optimize the filler addition amount and dispersion method, and deeply investigate the interaction mechanism between nanofillers and the epoxy resin matrix to overcome these challenges and further enhance the performance of coatings. Nanocrystalline cellulose (NCC), a renewable and highly crystalline natural polymer, possesses a one-dimensional nanorod structure, a high specific surface area, and excellent mechanical properties, making it an ideal nanofiller for improving the performance of epoxy resin coatings 19 . Nevertheless, the hydrophilic surface of NCC has poor compatibility with lipophilic epoxy resins, thereby limiting its application in epoxy resins 20 . To address the compatibility issue between NCC and epoxy resins, researchers have conducted extensive research. These efforts mainly center on the chemical modification of NCC and enhance the dispersibility of NCC in organic solvents and its compatibility with epoxy resins by introducing various functional groups 21 , 22 . For instance, the surface grafting modification of NCC using modifiers such as n-octadecyl isocyanate, hexanoyl chloride, lauroyl chloride, and stearyl chloride can enhance its dispersibility in organic solvents and its compatibility with the polymer matrix 23 , 24 . Additionally, hydrophobic groups and active amino groups can be introduced on the surface of NCC through the use of silane coupling agents like γ-(2,3-epoxy) propyltrimethoxysilane and poly(methylhydrogen)siloxane, further strengthening its interfacial interaction with epoxy resin and coating performance 25 , 26 . Inspired by previous studies, this research utilizes nanocrystalline cellulose (NCC) as a nanofiller and modifies it with an alkoxysilane coupling agent to enhance the compatibility and interfacial adhesion between NCC and epoxy resin. By introducing an alkoxysilane coupling agent, hydrophobic groups and active amino groups can be introduced on the surface of NCC, thereby improving its dispersibility in organic solvents and its reactivity with epoxy resin. In this study, the interface regulation mechanism and embedding dispersion mechanism of M-NCC and epoxy resin will be systematically explored to construct a metal protective coating with outstanding wear resistance, mechanical stability, and hydrophobicity. Simultaneously, the performance of the M-NCC/epoxy composite coating in terms of resistance to cold and hot cycles and solvent resistance, as well as the corrosion protection effect on Q235 carbon steel, will be evaluated through electrochemical impedance spectroscopy, coating surface contact angle, and optical morphology analysis. This study aims to provide theoretical support and practical guidance for the performance improvement of epoxy resin coatings and the development of novel anti-corrosion coatings.

Results and discussion Characterization of M-NCC epoxy coating Figure  1 a shows the ATR-FTIR spectra of M-NCC and pure NCC with different contents. The M-NCC showed two medium-intensity absorption peaks of -NH 2  at 3360 cm –1  and 3200 cm –1 . The introduction of amino groups was the grafting of APTMS in NCC, and the presence of amino groups can provide groups for the ring-opening reaction in epoxy resin. A C-H extensional vibration peak was observed at 2901 cm –1 , while the Si-O-C and Si-O-Si absorption peaks were observed at 1194 cm –1  and 1095 cm –1 , respectively, indicating that APTMS and HDTMS were successfully grafted onto NCC. In the ATR-FTIR spectrum of pure epoxy resin, characteristic absorption peaks of epoxy groups and C-O-C groups were observed at 916 cm –1  and 1185 cm –1  (as shown in Fig.  1 b). Upon addition of M-NCC, these two absorption peaks were observed to weaken or disappear, suggesting that the M-NCC underwent a ring-opening reaction in epoxy resin. The TGA curves of the epoxy coating and the M-3% NCC/EP coating in Fig.  1 c show that both coatings gradually lose weight at 50 ~ 160 °C due to the evaporation of absorbed moisture. Between 200 °C and 300 °C, the weight-loss rate of the M-3% NCC/EP coating was slower than that of the epoxy coating due to the presence of a Si-C bond in the M-NCC doped with epoxy resin. This bond has a high bonding energy, which delays thermal decomposition. Above 300 °C, the epoxy resin decomposed more rapidly, while the M-3% NCC/EP coating promoted the formation of silicon carbide and SiO 2  at high temperature 27 , thereby enhancing the thermal stability of the coating. Furthermore, the DTG curve (Fig.  1 d) shows that the degradation temperature of the M-3% NCC/EP coating is higher than that of the pure epoxy coating, suggesting that the M-3% NCC/EP coating has better thermal stability. Upon comparison of the residual weights of the two coatings after thermogravimetric analysis, it was observed that the residual amount of the coating with M-3% NCC/EP added was greater than that of the pure epoxy coating. This was attributed to the flame-retardant properties of the silanized NCC, which generated the volatile products during the decomposition process that acted as a mass transfer barrier to prevent thermal decomposition 28 .

 Wettability of M-NCC epoxy coating Pure EP coating is inherently hydrophilic, as evidenced by its low WCA of 65.7° (Fig.  4 a). When unmodified NCC (a hydrophilic material) is added alone, the WCA slightly decreases to 62.9° (Fig.  4 b), consistent with the hydrophilic nature of both components. In contrast (Fig.  4 c), the introduction of hydrophobic RSiO into EP improves hydrophobicity, increasing the WCA to 94.1°—this is attributed to the incorporation of hydrophobic functional groups from RSiO, which reduce surface affinity for water. The M-NCC (functionalized with RSiO) combines the hydrophobicity of RSiO with the ability to introduce nanoscale roughness. At a low loading of 0.5%, the M-NCC disperses uniformly, creating micro/nanoscale protrusions on the coating surface. According to the Cassie-Baxter principle, this roughness amplifies the hydrophobic effect of the RSiO component: water droplets are partially supported by air pockets trapped in the rough structure, reducing contact with the solid surface and increasing the WCA to 100.9°—a value higher than that of EP + RSiO (94.1°), which lacks such roughness. As the content of M-NCC increases (Fig.  4 e–g), the surface roughness further intensifies due to the accumulation of more nanoscale particles. This leads to a gradual increase in WCA, reaching 107.4° at 5% loading, as the enhanced roughness continues to synergize with the hydrophobic surface chemistry. This trend confirms that the combination of hydrophobic functionalization and controlled roughness is key to improving wettability.

 Anticorrosion performance of M-NCC epoxy coating in sodium chloride Figure  7  shows the electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (Nyquist diagram, Bode diagram) of epoxy coating and 0.5%, 1%, 3%, and 5% M-NCC/epoxy coatings subjected to 60 cycles of heating from 100 °C to 25 °C in a 3.5% NaCl solution, with each cycle consisting of 2 h at 100 °C, followed by 2 hours at 25 °C. In the Bode diagram for the electrochemical impedance spectroscopy of 0.5%, 1%, 3%, and 5% M-NCC coatings (Fig.  7 b 2 , c 2 , d 2  and e 2 ), the high-frequency impedance values of these four coatings were nearly linear with frequency prior to the high/low temperature cycles, while the impedance value at low frequency was higher, reaching 10 10 Ω cm 2 . In the phase angle diagram (Fig.  7 b 3 , c 3 , d 3  and e 3 ), it was also observed that the phase angle in the high-frequency region was approximately − 90°, resulting in a capacitive response in the Bode diagram of the coating. This shows that the epoxy coating system incorporating M-NCC forms a high-impedance shielding layer, demonstrating excellent shielding properties. In the pure epoxy coating (Fig.  7 a 2 ), although the initial impedance value was high (10 9  Ω cm 2 ), as the number of high/low temperature cycles in sodium chloride solution increased to 15 times, the diameter of the capacitive reactance arc decreased (Fig.  7 a 1 ), and the impedance value dropped from 10 9  Ω cm 2  to 10 7  Ω cm 2 . Additionally, the phase angle curve shifted towards lower frequencies (Fig.  7 a 3 ), indicating that the electrolyte solution had penetrated into the surface of Q235 carbon steel, thereby accelerating the metal corrosion due to the presence of corrosive media. When the number of cycles increased to 40 times, the phase angle curve decreased, and the impedance value of the pure epoxy coating dropped to 10 3  Ω cm 2  after 60 cycles, while the impedance value of bare carbon steel in 3.5% NaCl solution was 600 ~ 1000 Ω cm 2 . This indicated that the protective performance of the pure epoxy coating on Q235 carbon steel was compromised after 60 cycles of high and low temperatures in the sodium chloride solution. During the high and low temperature cycles, thermal stress was induced in the coating. Thermal stress resulted in cracks in the coating, and in severe cases, the coating may peel off, creating a pathway for corrosive media such as Cl − , H 2 O, and O 2  to reach the metal surface 29 , 30 . In the M-0.5% NCC/EP coating and the M-1% NCC/EP coating, after 3 cycles, the diameter of the capacitive reactance arc in the Nyquist diagram decreased, and the impedance modulus showed a significant reduction at both high and low frequencies (Fig.  7 b 1  and  c 1 ). During the 3–60 cycles, the impedance values and phase angles in the frequency range of 10 − 2 ~10 0  Hz decreased, and several impedance spectra in 10 0 ~10 4  Hz overlapped, indicating that the impedance values and phase angles at the high frequency end did not change much during the cycle (Fig.  7 b 2 , b 3,  c 2,  and c 3 ). This shows that the addition of M-NCC can enhance the corrosion resistance of epoxy resin coating under the combined effects of thermal cycling and corrosive media. When the addition amount of NCC modified by silane coupling agent increased to 3%, specifically in the M-3% NCC/EP coating, after 15 cycles, the impedance value and phase angle in the Bode diagram of the electrochemical impedance spectroscopy of the M-3% NCC/EP coating did not show significant decreases at both high and low frequencies (Fig.  7 d 2  and d 3 ). After 40 cycles of thermal cycling, the diameter of the capacitive reactance arc decreased noticeably (Fig.  7 d 1 ), and the impedance modulus at low frequencies decreased by nearly an order of magnitude (Fig.  7 d 2 ), but the phase angle at the high frequency end did not change much (Fig.  7 d 3 ). This proves that increasing the addition of M-NCC from 0.5 to 3% has a positive correlation with the thermal cycling resistance and corrosion resistance of the coating. The diameter of the capacitive reactance arc in the Nyquist plot of the M-5% NCC/EP coating is smaller compared to that of the M-3% NCC/EP coating, and this decrease becomes even more pronounced after 15 heating cycles (Fig.  7 e 1 ). The impedance spectrum change pattern of the M-5% NCC/EP coating, subjected to three cycles of heating at 100 ~ 25 °C, is similar to that of the M-NCC epoxy coating (0.5%, 1%, and 3%). However, after 15 cycles, the impedance value in the tested frequency range showed a significant decrease (Fig.  7 e 2 ), and the phase angle curve also declined (Fig.  7 e 3 ). This indicated that the electrolyte solution had penetrated the M-5% NCC/EP coating to a saturated state. As the number of cycles increased, the impedance value of the coating dropped to 10 5  Ω cm 2 , indicating that the thermal cycle and the electrolyte can jointly enhance the corrosion of Q235 carbon steel once the solution had saturated the coating. For further analysis of the electrochemical impedance spectroscopy of different coating samples, equivalent circuit fitting processing is used. The equivalent circuit diagram (Fig.  8 a) is applicable to the early and middle stages of immersion of most organic coatings. At this stage, the electrolyte solution penetrated into the coating and the metal surface through the micropores on the coating surface. Figure  8 b is applicable to the uniform penetration of the electrolyte solution into the coating. In the coating system, due to the diffusion effect caused by factors such as surface heterogeneity and roughness, the double layer capacitance (C dl ) of the electrode and electrolyte interface cannot be ideally represented by a capacitance element 31 , but can be replaced by a constant phase element (CPE). When the epoxy coating was subjected to cyclic heating in air from 100 °C to 25 °C, the impedance modulus |Z| 0.01  Hz of the epoxy coating decreased from 2.11 × 10 10  Ω cm 2  to 2.44 × 10 7  Ω cm 2 ; while the impedance value of the composite epoxy coating modified with the silane coupling agent did not show a significant overall decrease after 60 cycles. This is attributed to the fact that NCC has a low thermal expansion coefficient, and silanized NCC can enhance its thermal stability. Silanized NCC doped in epoxy resin coatings can reduce the internal stress of the coating induced by alternating high and low temperatures, reduce the damage caused by coating cracks due to internal stress, and thus enhancing the protective performance of the coating in a thermal cycling environment. By fitting the equivalent circuit diagram of Fig.  8 a, the changes in R f  and R ct  of different coating samples were obtained, as shown in Fig.  10 ; Table  3 . The resistance Rf of both the epoxy coating and the M-NCC coating increased with the number of thermal cycles, exhibiting a trend of initially increasing and then decreasing. Due to the non-uniformity of the cross-linking nodes of the epoxy resin itself, the epoxy resin caused the nodes to be redefined at the higher temperature of the hot and cold cycle, which can enhance the cross-linking density of the epoxy resin and improve the bonding strength between the epoxy resin and the metal matrix 38 . The epoxy coating decreased after 15 cycles, while the composite epoxy coating with 0.5% and 1% M-NCC decreased after 40 cycles. When the M-NCC was added as a filler to the epoxy resin, it was combined with the epoxy resin in the form of a chemical bond, which can reduce the thermal expansion of the epoxy resin at higher temperatures. With the increase in the amount of M-NCC doping, the internal stress of the polymer-filler interface also increased. Characterization of M-NCC epoxy coating Figure  1 a shows the ATR-FTIR spectra of M-NCC and pure NCC with different contents. The M-NCC showed two medium-intensity absorption peaks of -NH 2  at 3360 cm –1  and 3200 cm –1 . The introduction of amino groups was the grafting of APTMS in NCC, and the presence of amino groups can provide groups for the ring-opening reaction in epoxy resin. A C-H extensional vibration peak was observed at 2901 cm –1 , while the Si-O-C and Si-O-Si absorption peaks were observed at 1194 cm –1  and 1095 cm –1 , respectively, indicating that APTMS and HDTMS were successfully grafted onto NCC. In the ATR-FTIR spectrum of pure epoxy resin, characteristic absorption peaks of epoxy groups and C-O-C groups were observed at 916 cm –1  and 1185 cm –1  (as shown in Fig.  1 b). Upon addition of M-NCC, these two absorption peaks were observed to weaken or disappear, suggesting that the M-NCC underwent a ring-opening reaction in epoxy resin. The TGA curves of the epoxy coating and the M-3% NCC/EP coating in Fig.  1 c show that both coatings gradually lose weight at 50 ~ 160 °C due to the evaporation of absorbed moisture. Between 200 °C and 300 °C, the weight-loss rate of the M-3% NCC/EP coating was slower than that of the epoxy coating due to the presence of a Si-C bond in the M-NCC doped with epoxy resin. This bond has a high bonding energy, which delays thermal decomposition. Above 300 °C, the epoxy resin decomposed more rapidly, while the M-3% NCC/EP coating promoted the formation of silicon carbide and SiO 2  at high temperature 27 , thereby enhancing the thermal stability of the coating. Furthermore, the DTG curve (Fig.  1 d) shows that the degradation temperature of the M-3% NCC/EP coating is higher than that of the pure epoxy coating, suggesting that the M-3% NCC/EP coating has better thermal stability. Upon comparison of the residual weights of the two coatings after thermogravimetric analysis, it was observed that the residual amount of the coating with M-3% NCC/EP added was greater than that of the pure epoxy coating. This was attributed to the flame-retardant properties of the silanized NCC, which generated the volatile products during the decomposition process that acted as a mass transfer barrier to prevent thermal decomposition 28 .

Wettability of M-NCC epoxy coating Pure EP coating is inherently hydrophilic, as evidenced by its low WCA of 65.7° (Fig.  4 a). When unmodified NCC (a hydrophilic material) is added alone, the WCA slightly decreases to 62.9° (Fig.  4 b), consistent with the hydrophilic nature of both components. In contrast (Fig.  4 c), the introduction of hydrophobic RSiO into EP improves hydrophobicity, increasing the WCA to 94.1°—this is attributed to the incorporation of hydrophobic functional groups from RSiO, which reduce surface affinity for water. The M-NCC (functionalized with RSiO) combines the hydrophobicity of RSiO with the ability to introduce nanoscale roughness. At a low loading of 0.5%, the M-NCC disperses uniformly, creating micro/nanoscale protrusions on the coating surface. According to the Cassie-Baxter principle, this roughness amplifies the hydrophobic effect of the RSiO component: water droplets are partially supported by air pockets trapped in the rough structure, reducing contact with the solid surface and increasing the WCA to 100.9°—a value higher than that of EP + RSiO (94.1°), which lacks such roughness. As the content of M-NCC increases (Fig.  4 e–g), the surface roughness further intensifies due to the accumulation of more nanoscale particles. This leads to a gradual increase in WCA, reaching 107.4° at 5% loading, as the enhanced roughness continues to synergize with the hydrophobic surface chemistry. This trend confirms that the combination of hydrophobic functionalization and controlled roughness is key to improving wettability.

Anticorrosion performance of M-NCC epoxy coating in sodium chloride Figure  7  shows the electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (Nyquist diagram, Bode diagram) of epoxy coating and 0.5%, 1%, 3%, and 5% M-NCC/epoxy coatings subjected to 60 cycles of heating from 100 °C to 25 °C in a 3.5% NaCl solution, with each cycle consisting of 2 h at 100 °C, followed by 2 hours at 25 °C. In the Bode diagram for the electrochemical impedance spectroscopy of 0.5%, 1%, 3%, and 5% M-NCC coatings (Fig.  7 b 2 , c 2 , d 2  and e 2 ), the high-frequency impedance values of these four coatings were nearly linear with frequency prior to the high/low temperature cycles, while the impedance value at low frequency was higher, reaching 10 10 Ω cm 2 . In the phase angle diagram (Fig.  7 b 3 , c 3 , d 3  and e 3 ), it was also observed that the phase angle in the high-frequency region was approximately − 90°, resulting in a capacitive response in the Bode diagram of the coating. This shows that the epoxy coating system incorporating M-NCC forms a high-impedance shielding layer, demonstrating excellent shielding properties. In the pure epoxy coating (Fig.  7 a 2 ), although the initial impedance value was high (10 9  Ω cm 2 ), as the number of high/low temperature cycles in sodium chloride solution increased to 15 times, the diameter of the capacitive reactance arc decreased (Fig.  7 a 1 ), and the impedance value dropped from 10 9  Ω cm 2  to 10 7  Ω cm 2 . Additionally, the phase angle curve shifted towards lower frequencies (Fig.  7 a 3 ), indicating that the electrolyte solution had penetrated into the surface of Q235 carbon steel, thereby accelerating the metal corrosion due to the presence of corrosive media. When the number of cycles increased to 40 times, the phase angle curve decreased, and the impedance value of the pure epoxy coating dropped to 10 3  Ω cm 2  after 60 cycles, while the impedance value of bare carbon steel in 3.5% NaCl solution was 600 ~ 1000 Ω cm 2 . This indicated that the protective performance of the pure epoxy coating on Q235 carbon steel was compromised after 60 cycles of high and low temperatures in the sodium chloride solution. During the high and low temperature cycles, thermal stress was induced in the coating. Thermal stress resulted in cracks in the coating, and in severe cases, the coating may peel off, creating a pathway for corrosive media such as Cl − , H 2 O, and O 2  to reach the metal surface 29 , 30 . In the M-0.5% NCC/EP coating and the M-1% NCC/EP coating, after 3 cycles, the diameter of the capacitive reactance arc in the Nyquist diagram decreased, and the impedance modulus showed a significant reduction at both high and low frequencies (Fig.  7 b 1  and  c 1 ). During the 3–60 cycles, the impedance values and phase angles in the frequency range of 10 − 2 ~10 0  Hz decreased, and several impedance spectra in 10 0 ~10 4  Hz overlapped, indicating that the impedance values and phase angles at the high frequency end did not change much during the cycle (Fig.  7 b 2 , b 3,  c 2,  and c 3 ). This shows that the addition of M-NCC can enhance the corrosion resistance of epoxy resin coating under the combined effects of thermal cycling and corrosive media. When the addition amount of NCC modified by silane coupling agent increased to 3%, specifically in the M-3% NCC/EP coating, after 15 cycles, the impedance value and phase angle in the Bode diagram of the electrochemical impedance spectroscopy of the M-3% NCC/EP coating did not show significant decreases at both high and low frequencies (Fig.  7 d 2  and d 3 ). After 40 cycles of thermal cycling, the diameter of the capacitive reactance arc decreased noticeably (Fig.  7 d 1 ), and the impedance modulus at low frequencies decreased by nearly an order of magnitude (Fig.  7 d 2 ), but the phase angle at the high frequency end did not change much (Fig.  7 d 3 ). This proves that increasing the addition of M-NCC from 0.5 to 3% has a positive correlation with the thermal cycling resistance and corrosion resistance of the coating. The diameter of the capacitive reactance arc in the Nyquist plot of the M-5% NCC/EP coating is smaller compared to that of the M-3% NCC/EP coating, and this decrease becomes even more pronounced after 15 heating cycles (Fig.  7 e 1 ). The impedance spectrum change pattern of the M-5% NCC/EP coating, subjected to three cycles of heating at 100 ~ 25 °C, is similar to that of the M-NCC epoxy coating (0.5%, 1%, and 3%). However, after 15 cycles, the impedance value in the tested frequency range showed a significant decrease (Fig.  7 e 2 ), and the phase angle curve also declined (Fig.  7 e 3 ). This indicated that the electrolyte solution had penetrated the M-5% NCC/EP coating to a saturated state. As the number of cycles increased, the impedance value of the coating dropped to 10 5  Ω cm 2 , indicating that the thermal cycle and the electrolyte can jointly enhance the corrosion of Q235 carbon steel once the solution had saturated the coating. For further analysis of the electrochemical impedance spectroscopy of different coating samples, equivalent circuit fitting processing is used. The equivalent circuit diagram (Fig.  8 a) is applicable to the early and middle stages of immersion of most organic coatings. At this stage, the electrolyte solution penetrated into the coating and the metal surface through the micropores on the coating surface. Figure  8 b is applicable to the uniform penetration of the electrolyte solution into the coating. In the coating system, due to the diffusion effect caused by factors such as surface heterogeneity and roughness, the double layer capacitance (C dl ) of the electrode and electrolyte interface cannot be ideally represented by a capacitance element 31 , but can be replaced by a constant phase element (CPE). Thermal cycling performance of M-NCC epoxy coating Figure  9  (a 1 -e 1 ) show the Nyquist diagram of the epoxy coating, M-0.5% NCC/EP, M-1% NCC/EP, M-3% NCC/EP, and M-5% NCC/EP coatings, respectively, and Fig.  9  (a 2 -e 2 ) and Fig.  9  (a 3 -e 3 ) show the Bode diagram. When the epoxy coating was subjected to cyclic heating in air from 100 °C to 25 °C, the impedance modulus |Z| 0.01  Hz of the epoxy coating decreased from 2.11 × 10 10  Ω cm 2  to 2.44 × 10 7  Ω cm 2 ; while the impedance value of the composite epoxy coating modified with the silane coupling agent did not show a significant overall decrease after 60 cycles. This is attributed to the fact that NCC has a low thermal expansion coefficient, and silanized NCC can enhance its thermal stability. Silanized NCC doped in epoxy resin coatings can reduce the internal stress of the coating induced by alternating high and low temperatures, reduce the damage caused by coating cracks due to internal stress, and thus enhancing the protective performance of the coating in a thermal cycling environment. By fitting the equivalent circuit diagram of Fig.  8 a, the changes in R f  and R ct  of different coating samples were obtained, as shown in Fig.  10 ; Table  3 . The resistance Rf of both the epoxy coating and the M-NCC coating increased with the number of thermal cycles, exhibiting a trend of initially increasing and then decreasing. Due to the non-uniformity of the cross-linking nodes of the epoxy resin itself, the epoxy resin caused the nodes to be redefined at the higher temperature of the hot and cold cycle, which can enhance the cross-linking density of the epoxy resin and improve the bonding strength between the epoxy resin and the metal matrix 38 . The epoxy coating decreased after 15 cycles, while the composite epoxy coating with 0.5% and 1% M-NCC decreased after 40 cycles. When the M-NCC was added as a filler to the epoxy resin, it was combined with the epoxy resin in the form of a chemical bond, which can reduce the thermal expansion of the epoxy resin at higher temperatures. With the increase in the amount of M-NCC doping, the internal stress of the polymer-filler interface also increased. When the temperature rose, the internal stress led to cracks in the coating, thereby reducing the protective performance of the coating.

Conclusion In this study, NCC was modified using HDTMS and APTMS, and the content of M-NCC in epoxy resin (E44) was adjusted to successfully prepare a series of composite epoxy coatings (M-NCC/EP) with 0.5%, 1%, 3%, and 5% M-NCC. These coatings were applied to the surfaces of carbon steel by spraying to enhance their chemical stability, wettability, solvent resistance, corrosion resistance and thermal cycling resistance. Firstly, using FTIR, ATR and XPS characterization techniques, we confirmed that HDTMS and APTMS had been successfully grafted onto the NCC surface, and the thermogravimetric analysis showed that M-NCC significantly enhanced its thermal stability. Secondly, the results of the WCA test showed that all epoxy coatings containing different amounts of M-NCC exhibited hydrophobic characteristics (WCA>90°), and the contact angle showed an increasing trend with increasing amounts of M-NCC added, indicating that the hydrophobicity of the coatings was effectively enhanced. Furthermore, through 3D morphology profile and optical morphology characterization, it was observed that in ethyl acetate and DMF solvents, with increasing amounts of M-NCC, the swelling and shrinkage of the epoxy coating were significantly reduced, thereby enhancing the solvent resistance of the coating. The results of the EIS tests showed that after 60 cycles of high and low temperatures in 3.5% NaCl solution and in air, the M-NCC composite epoxy coating exhibited better protective performance than pure organic epoxy coating. In particular, when the addition amount of M-NCC was 1% and 3%, the protective effect of the coating was the most significant. This was mainly due to the low expansion coefficient of NCC and the close bonding between M-NCC and epoxy resin through chemical bonds, which effectively reduced the thermal expansion and internal stress of epoxy resin during thermal cycling. In addition, the hydrophobicity of the M-NCC/EP coating and the filled M-NCC contributed to blocking the invasion of corrosive media, further enhancing the protective performance of the coating. To sum up, this study successfully developed a M-NCC/epoxy composite coating with excellent solvent resistance, corrosion resistance and thermal cycling resistance by utilizing green and environmentally friendly nanocrystalline cellulose and a silane coupling agent with low production cost. This achievement not only provides a new strategy for enhancing the performance of epoxy coatings, but also offers an important theoretical and practical basis for expanding their application in extreme environments.
